docs.title: CS101: ICS
docs.text:
CS101-ICS stands for Introduction to Computer Systems, but this project is not a conventional university-level course.

Instead, it’s a personal documentation site that explores computing fundamentals, digital tools, and practical workflows that help people better understand and utilize information technology.

docs.title: 🌐 Overview
docs.text:
CS101-ICS is a long-term documentation project designed as both a learning notebook and a knowledge portal. It combines elements of a computer science introduction, a “missing semester” guide, and a toolbox for document and system solutions.

Rather than following a strict academic syllabus, this project grows organically — documenting tools, workflows, and foundational concepts that form the core of modern computing literacy.

docs.title: 🧭 Project Philosophy
docs.text:
“To understand computers not just as machines, but as tools of thought.”

The philosophy behind CS101-ICS is simple:

  • Practicality over theory — learn by exploring tools and systems.
  • Documentation as learning — writing about concepts helps solidify understanding.
  • Bridging academia and practice — connect core CS ideas with real-world applications.

docs.title: 🧰 Future Directions
docs.text:
Planned topics include:

  • Computing essentials — binary, logic, hardware, and operating systems basics.
  • Software tools — shells, editors, scripting, and automation.
  • Version control & collaboration — Git, GitHub, and open-source practices.
  • System thinking — how components of modern computing fit together.

Each topic will be written with both clarity and depth, balancing professional rigor and accessible explanations.

docs.title: Documentation Solutions
docs.text:
This section discusses how different ecosystems handle document editing, conversion, and collaboration.

It compares:

  • Microsoft Office – the classic integrated productivity suite.
  • Apple iWork – a minimalist, design-focused office solution.
  • Markdown / LaTeX – text-based, developer-friendly document workflows.
  • Pandoc – the universal document converter that bridges them all.

The goal is to understand how different solutions represent the same fundamental problem: information expression and transformation.

From Office to Markdown: The Evolution of Document Solutions

When we talk about Office software, most people immediately think of Microsoft Word, Excel, or PowerPoint. But in reality, Office is not just a group of programs — it’s a complete solution for document creation, editing, and management. Different companies have their own interpretations of what an “office solution” should look like, and over time, the concept has evolved from traditional desktop software to flexible, open, and code-driven ecosystems.

docs.title: 1. What Is an “Office Solution”?
docs.text:
An office suite is essentially a document productivity solution — a collection of tools that help users create, process, and share information efficiently. These tools typically include:

  • Word processors – for writing and editing documents

  • Spreadsheets – for organizing and analyzing data

  • Presentation software – for designing slideshows and talks

  • Email, database, or drawing tools – for specialized communication and record keeping

What makes these suites solutions instead of just individual apps is that they share consistent design, file formats, and workflows, forming a unified ecosystem.

docs.title: 2. Different Companies, Different Philosophies
docs.text:
Each company defines “office productivity” differently. As a result, their solutions reflect distinct priorities and design philosophies.

Company Representative Products Core Philosophy Microsoft Office 365 (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook) Feature-rich and enterprise-oriented; prioritizes compatibility and automation Apple iWork (Pages, Numbers, Keynote) Elegant, minimalist, and visually appealing; tailored for individuals and creatives LibreOffice Writer, Calc, Impress Open-source and cross-platform; a free alternative to proprietary tools Google Docs, Sheets, Slides Cloud-first collaboration; simplicity and real-time teamwork

Each of these ecosystems aims to solve the same fundamental problem — how to help people create and communicate effectively — but their approaches differ according to target users and technology priorities.

docs.title: 3. Markdown and LaTeX: The Text-Based Alternatives
docs.text:
Beyond traditional office suites, there exists another powerful family of solutions based on plain text and structured markup — namely, Markdown and LaTeX.

While Office tools emphasize what you see is what you get (WYSIWYG), these systems emphasize what you see is what you mean (WYSIWYM). They separate content from presentation, allowing for flexible and automated formatting.

Toolchain Core Idea Typical Use Cases Markdown + Pandoc / MkDocs / Typst Simple syntax, easy to read and convert Notes, documentation, blogs, reports LaTeX + BibTeX / Beamer Precise typesetting, professional layout control Academic papers, theses, research slides

With the right pipeline, you can turn a plain-text Markdown file into a styled PDF, website, or presentation — all without opening a GUI editor. This is why developers, writers, and researchers often prefer such text-driven solutions.

docs.title: 4. From Software to Ecosystem Thinking
docs.text:
When we shift our view from “software” to “solution,” we start to see that an office suite is not just about editing files — it’s about how information is created, formatted, shared, and preserved.

An office solution includes:

  • A set of coordinated tools

  • Standardized document formats

  • Cloud or local collaboration systems

  • User habits and conventions built around them

By this definition:

  • Microsoft Office is a commercial, closed-source enterprise solution.

  • LibreOffice is a community-driven, open-source counterpart.

  • Markdown and LaTeX ecosystems are open, modular, and programmable solutions built on text files and conversion tools.

docs.title: 5. The Future of Document Solutions
docs.text:
In the modern era, the boundaries between these systems are becoming blurred. You can edit Markdown in Visual Studio Code and export it to Word or PDF; Google Docs can export to LaTeX-compatible formats; and tools like Obsidian, Notion, or Typst are redefining what “writing” means in a digital world.

Ultimately, the best solution is the one that matches your workflow:

  • If you value visual design and simplicity, Apple’s iWork might be ideal.

  • If you prioritize compatibility and automation, Microsoft Office still dominates.

  • If you want openness, transparency, and full control, Markdown or LaTeX ecosystems are unmatched.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
From Microsoft Office to Markdown, every office suite and markup language represents a different answer to the same question:

How can we express, organize, and share ideas effectively?

As technology evolves, the tools may change — but the goal remains the same: to help humans turn thoughts into documents, and documents into communication.

docs.title: Understanding Pandoc: The Universal Document Converter
docs.text: In computer science and software engineering, we often deal with a wide variety of file formats — Markdown for notes, LaTeX for papers, HTML for web pages, and PDF for reports. Managing and converting among them can be frustrating. This is where Pandoc comes in — a powerful, flexible, and open-source tool that bridges the gap between formats, making document conversion almost effortless.

docs.title: 1. What Is Pandoc?
docs.text:
Pandoc is often called the “Swiss army knife” of document converters. It’s a command-line program that can read documents in one format and convert them to another — accurately, efficiently, and with remarkable customization.

Developed by John MacFarlane, a philosophy professor at the University of California, Berkeley, Pandoc started as a Markdown converter but has grown into a universal translator for text-based documents. Today, it supports dozens of input and output formats, including:

  • Input formats: Markdown, HTML, LaTeX, Word (.docx), EPUB, reStructuredText, and more

  • Output formats: PDF, DOCX, HTML, LaTeX, slides (Reveal.js), and even PowerPoint

For example, you can turn a Markdown file into a polished PDF or a slide deck with a single command:

pandoc mynote.md -o mynote.pdf

docs.title: 2. Why Do We Need Pandoc?
docs.text: In computer science and academia, different tools and workflows use different file formats. Pandoc eliminates the need to manually reformat your work every time you move between environments.

docs.title: ✅ Typical use cases:
docs.text:
• Converting Markdown notes into HTML pages for a course website

  • Turning a LaTeX report into a Word document for submission

  • Generating PDF handouts from Markdown lecture notes

  • Building slide presentations with Reveal.js or Beamer

  • Creating EPUB e-books from plain text

This flexibility makes Pandoc especially popular among developers, researchers, educators, and technical writers.

docs.title: 3. How Pandoc Works
docs.text:
Pandoc follows a simple but elegant model:

  1. Parse the input: It reads your document and converts it into an internal abstract syntax tree (AST).

  2. Transform the AST: It applies filters, metadata, or styling rules if needed.

  3. Write the output: Finally, it generates the document in your chosen format.

This architecture makes Pandoc extensible and programmable — you can write custom filters (in Lua, Python, or Haskell) to modify or enhance documents during conversion.

docs.text:
Pandoc is cross-platform and runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux.

For example, on macOS you can install it using Homebrew:

brew install pandoc

On Linux:

sudo apt install pandoc

Or download binaries from the official Pandoc website.

docs.title: ⚙️ Basic Usage
docs.text:
The simplest usage pattern looks like this:

pandoc input.md -o output.pdf

You can specify formats explicitly:

pandoc -f markdown -t html -o page.html input.md

where:

  • -f means “from” (the input format)

  • -t means “to” (the output format)

  • -o specifies the output file name

You can also add metadata, templates, and CSS to control the final look.

docs.title: 5. Going Further: Templates and Filters
docs.text:
Pandoc allows deep customization. You can define templates to give all your documents a consistent layout or use filters to automate transformations.

For instance, if you want every code block in your notes to have syntax highlighting, or every image to include a caption automatically — a small Lua filter can do that for you.

Pandoc’s templating system also integrates with LaTeX and HTML engines, letting you fine-tune professional documents with minimal effort.

docs.title: 6. Integration in CS Workflows
docs.text:
Pandoc fits perfectly into a CS101 or software documentation environment:

  • Combine Markdown lecture notes with diagrams and export to HTML for your course website.

  • Generate PDF lab reports automatically from Markdown templates.

  • Use Pandoc in a Makefile or GitHub Action to publish updated docs whenever you push changes.

Because it’s purely command-line based, Pandoc can easily become part of automated build or publishing pipelines.

docs.title: 7. Conclusion
docs.text:
Pandoc embodies the best of open-source design — simplicity, power, and flexibility. By mastering it early, you gain a tool that will remain useful far beyond CS101 — in academic writing, documentation, research, and professional development.

In short:

If your text is structured, Pandoc can transform it.

📝 A Complete Introduction to Markdown (with Examples)

Markdown is one of the simplest yet most powerful markup languages for writing on the web. From GitHub READMEs to personal blogs and documentation sites, Markdown has become the universal format for text content that’s both easy to write and easy to read.

In this post, we’ll dive into what Markdown is, why it’s so popular, and give you a hands-on tutorial to start writing it right away.

docs.title: 🌱 What Is Markdown?
docs.text:
Markdown is a lightweight markup language created by John Gruber in 2004. Its goal was simple:

To make writing for the web as easy as writing plain text.

That means instead of learning complicated HTML tags like:

<h1>This is a heading</h1>
<p>This is a paragraph</p>

you can just write:

# This is a heading
This is a paragraph.

And Markdown will automatically convert it to the correct HTML when rendered.

docs.title: 💡 Why Use Markdown?
docs.text:
Markdown became so popular because it’s:

  • Readable as plain text — no messy tags.

  • Fast to learn — just a few rules to remember.

  • Portable — works on GitHub, Reddit, Notion, Obsidian, MkDocs, and many more tools.

  • Perfect for version control — since it’s text-based, you can track changes easily with Git.

If you’ve ever written documentation, notes, or a README file, Markdown is your best friend.

docs.title: ✍️ Basic Syntax
docs.text: Let’s go through the most common Markdown elements one by one.

docs.title: 1. Headings
docs.text:
Use the # symbol followed by a space.

# Heading 1
## Heading 2
### Heading 3
#### Heading 4

docs.title: 2. Paragraphs and Line Breaks
docs.text:
Just type your text normally. Leave an empty line between paragraphs.

This is the first paragraph.

This is another paragraph.

To force a line break, end a line with two spaces or use <br>.

docs.title: 3. Bold and Italic
docs.text:
**Bold text**
*Italic text*
***Bold and italic***

Result: Bold text Italic text Bold and italic

docs.title: 4. Lists
docs.text:
Unordered lists:

- Apple
- Banana
  - Sub-item
  - Another sub-item

Ordered lists:

1. First item
2. Second item
3. Third item

docs.title: 5. Links and Images
docs.text:
Links:

[OpenAI](https://www.openai.com)

Images:

![Alt text](https://example.com/image.jpg)

docs.title: 6. Blockquotes
docs.text:
Use > to create quotes:

> Markdown makes writing simple.

Markdown makes writing simple.

docs.title: 7. Code
docs.text:
Inline code:

Use `print()` to show output.

Use print() to show output.

Code blocks:

```python
def hello():
    print("Hello, Markdown!")
```

Rendered:

def hello():
    print("Hello, Markdown!")

docs.title: 8. Tables
docs.text:
| Name | Age | City |
|------|-----|------|
| Alice | 25 | London |
| Bob   | 30 | New York |

Output:

Name Age City Alice 25 London Bob 30 New York

docs.title: 9. Horizontal Rule
docs.text:
Use three or more dashes --- or asterisks ***.

---

docs.title: 10. Task Lists (GitHub-style)
docs.text:
- [x] Write Markdown post  
- [ ] Publish on blog

Rendered:

  • [x] Write Markdown post
  • [ ] Publish on blog

docs.title: ⚙️ Extended Markdown
docs.text:
Some platforms add extended syntax — for example:

  • Tables, checkboxes, and emoji (GitHub Flavored Markdown)

  • Math equations using LaTeX ($E = mc^2$)

  • Footnotes, definition lists, and callouts (in MkDocs, Obsidian, etc.)

For example, in MkDocs Material, you can even create admonitions like this:

!!! tip "Pro Tip"
    You can write beautiful docs with Markdown and Material for MkDocs.

Which renders as a styled “Tip” box!

!!! tip "Pro Tip" You can write beautiful docs with Markdown and Material for MkDocs.

docs.title: MkDocs Material: A Modern Framework for Beautiful Documentation
docs.text: In the age of open-source software and distributed development, effective documentation has become as essential as code itself. Among the many tools designed to simplify technical writing, MkDocs Material stands out as a modern, elegant, and developer-friendly framework that brings together simplicity, power, and aesthetic appeal. It enables teams and individuals to build professional documentation websites using Markdown, while maintaining full control over structure, style, and deployment.

docs.title: 1. The Foundation: What Is MkDocs?
docs.text:
MkDocs is a static site generator written in Python, originally created to help developers turn Markdown files into clean, navigable documentation websites. Unlike complex content management systems, MkDocs requires no backend server or database. Instead, it converts Markdown content into a fully static HTML site, which can be easily deployed to platforms like GitHub Pages, Netlify, or any static hosting service.

Its key philosophy is “documentation as code.” By storing documentation alongside source code in a version-controlled repository, MkDocs encourages developers to write and maintain documentation just like they manage software — with versioning, reviews, and automation.

docs.title: 2. The Material Theme: Where Design Meets Function
docs.text:
The Material for MkDocs theme, developed by Martin Donath, transforms MkDocs into a visually stunning and highly functional documentation system. Inspired by Google’s Material Design principles, it offers a clean and modern interface, emphasizing usability, accessibility, and responsive design.

Some of its standout features include:

  • Responsive Layout: Optimized for mobile, tablet, and desktop, ensuring a consistent reading experience across devices.

  • Dark Mode: Built-in light/dark theme switching, with automatic or manual toggling.

  • Typography and Icons: Beautiful fonts, well-balanced spacing, and access to Material Design Icons for a polished look.

  • Instant Search: A powerful client-side search engine that indexes content as you write.

  • Versioning and Localization: Support for multi-version and multi-language documentation, making it ideal for large projects.

Material for MkDocs is more than a theme — it’s an ecosystem. Through extensive configuration options, built-in plugins, and well-documented customization APIs, it allows authors to tailor the user interface and user experience to their project’s identity.

docs.title: a. Markdown-Centric Workflow
docs.text: At the heart of MkDocs Material lies Markdown, the lightweight markup language known for its readability and simplicity. Writers can focus purely on content, using intuitive syntax to format text, add links, include code blocks, and create tables — without dealing with HTML or CSS.

docs.title: b. Developer-Friendly Configuration
docs.text: Configuration is handled through a single mkdocs.yml file. This YAML file defines site metadata, navigation structure, theme settings, and plugin integrations. It makes the documentation site declarative and reproducible, ensuring consistency across environments.

docs.title: c. Integrated Plugins
docs.text:
The ecosystem supports a range of plugins that extend functionality. For example:

  • search – Provides built-in full-text search.

  • git-revision-date-localized – Displays the last modified date from Git.

  • awesome-pages – Automatically manages navigation based on directory structure.

  • mkdocs-material-extensions – Adds custom Markdown syntax and features.

docs.title: d. Advanced Theming and Customization
docs.text: Material for MkDocs supports deep customization. Users can override colors, typography, and layouts using custom CSS or by extending theme templates. The theme also supports Jinja2 templating, enabling advanced users to inject dynamic behavior or UI logic.

docs.title: e. Instant Preview and CI/CD Integration
docs.text: With mkdocs serve, developers can preview changes locally with live reloading. For deployment, MkDocs integrates seamlessly into CI/CD pipelines, allowing automatic site generation and deployment on every commit.

docs.title: 4. Building a Site: A Quick Overview
docs.text:
Creating a MkDocs Material site typically involves a few straightforward steps:

  1. Install MkDocs and Material Theme:
pip install mkdocs-material
  1. Create a New Project:
mkdocs new my-docs
cd my-docs
  1. Edit the Configuration File (mkdocs.yml):
site_name: My Project Documentation
theme:
  name: material

  1. Write Markdown Files: Add .md files under the docs/ directory.

  2. Preview Locally:

mkdocs serve
  1. Build the Site:
mkdocs build
  1. Deploy Anywhere: The generated site/ folder can be uploaded to any static web host.

This simplicity is one of MkDocs Material’s greatest strengths — it eliminates the complexity of traditional documentation systems, letting writers focus on clarity and structure.

docs.title: 5. Ideal Use Cases
docs.text:
MkDocs Material has become the default choice for:

  • Open Source Projects – Tools like FastAPI, Typer, and Pydantic use it for their official docs.

  • Internal Knowledge Bases – Teams can build lightweight, private documentation portals.

  • Educational Resources – Teachers and students use it to publish notes and tutorials.

  • APIs and SDKs – Combined with Markdown-based API references and code snippets, it provides a developer-friendly format.

docs.title: 6. Why MkDocs Material Matters
docs.text:
In today’s digital landscape, documentation is often a product’s first impression. A well-structured, aesthetically pleasing, and accessible documentation site can define user experience. MkDocs Material bridges the gap between engineering efficiency and design excellence — making documentation not just functional, but delightful.

It embodies a philosophy of clarity through simplicity, aligning perfectly with modern software practices. Whether used by a solo developer or a large team, MkDocs Material democratizes documentation — ensuring that anyone with Markdown skills can publish beautiful, professional sites effortlessly.

docs.title: 7. Conclusion
docs.text:
MkDocs Material represents the evolution of documentation tooling. It merges the simplicity of Markdown, the robustness of MkDocs, and the elegance of Material Design into a unified platform. Beyond its technical brilliance, it nurtures a culture of maintainable, accessible, and visually appealing documentation — a cornerstone of any successful open-source or professional project.

In short, MkDocs Material doesn’t just help you write documentation — it helps you tell a story elegantly, transparently, and effectively.

docs.title: A Comprehensive Overview
docs.text: In the modern era of digital presentations, efficiency, flexibility, and visual appeal are paramount. Reveal.js is a powerful open-source framework that has redefined the way web-based presentations are created and delivered. Developed by Hakim El Hattab in 2011, Reveal.js leverages standard web technologies such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to provide a versatile and interactive platform for presenting content.

docs.title: 1. Background and Development
docs.text: Before Reveal.js, presentation tools were often confined to desktop applications like Microsoft PowerPoint or Apple Keynote. While functional, these applications lacked the flexibility and interactivity that modern web technologies could offer. Reveal.js emerged as a response to this limitation, offering a lightweight framework that enables developers and content creators to build slide decks directly in the browser. Its open-source nature has fostered a vibrant community, resulting in continuous enhancements and a variety of plugins.

docs.title: 2. Core Features
docs.text:
Reveal.js is celebrated for its rich feature set, which makes it a versatile tool for both educators and professionals. Some of its core features include:

  • Slide Structure and Navigation: Slides are structured using simple HTML elements, and navigation can be horizontal, vertical, or even nested. Users can move seamlessly between slides using keyboard keys, touch gestures, or links.

  • Themes and Customization: Reveal.js supports a variety of built-in themes, allowing presentations to be styled consistently. Users can also customize layouts, fonts, and colors using CSS, offering almost limitless visual flexibility.

  • Interactive Elements: Presenters can incorporate multimedia such as images, videos, and audio. Additionally, Reveal.js supports code syntax highlighting, Markdown integration, and embedded web content, enabling highly interactive and engaging presentations.

  • Transitions and Animations: The framework includes a range of slide transitions, from simple fades to complex 3D effects, enhancing the visual experience and helping maintain audience engagement.

  • Plugins and Extensions: Reveal.js offers a robust plugin ecosystem. Features such as speaker notes, math equations using MathJax, and real-time collaborative editing are possible through extensions, significantly expanding its capabilities.

docs.title: 3. Advantages Over Traditional Tools
docs.text:
One of the most significant advantages of Reveal.js is its web-native nature. Unlike desktop-based presentation tools, Reveal.js presentations can be easily shared via a URL, embedded in websites, or hosted on platforms like GitHub Pages. This facilitates accessibility and collaboration, particularly in remote or online learning environments. Additionally, the open-source aspect means that presentations are highly customizable without incurring licensing costs.

Another notable benefit is responsiveness. Reveal.js presentations automatically adapt to different screen sizes, making them compatible with desktops, tablets, and smartphones. This flexibility is essential in the modern landscape, where audiences may use a variety of devices.

docs.title: 4. Use Cases
docs.text:
Reveal.js is widely used across various domains:

  • Education: Teachers and lecturers use it to create interactive lecture slides, integrating multimedia and live code examples to enhance understanding.

  • Tech Conferences and Meetups: Developers and speakers leverage Reveal.js to deliver technical presentations with embedded live demos, syntax-highlighted code, and interactive diagrams.

  • Corporate Presentations: Companies utilize Reveal.js for project updates, pitches, and training sessions, benefiting from its flexibility and web-based sharing.

docs.title: 5. Limitations and Considerations
docs.text: Despite its many advantages, Reveal.js has certain limitations. Unlike software like PowerPoint, it requires knowledge of web technologies such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. This learning curve may deter non-technical users. Additionally, while the framework is powerful, extremely complex animations or multimedia-heavy slides can sometimes impact performance, especially on low-end devices.

docs.title: 6. Future Prospects
docs.text: Reveal.js continues to evolve. Its community-driven development ensures that it adapts to emerging trends in web development and presentation design. Future prospects include tighter integration with collaborative tools, enhanced accessibility features, and improved performance for media-rich presentations.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Reveal.js represents a paradigm shift in the world of digital presentations. By leveraging the flexibility of web technologies, it provides an open, interactive, and highly customizable platform that surpasses traditional desktop tools in many respects. Whether for education, professional development, or creative expression, Reveal.js offers a modern solution for those seeking engaging and dynamic presentations. Its combination of simplicity, power, and adaptability ensures that it remains a compelling choice for content creators worldwide.

docs.title: Quick Start with Reveal.js
docs.text: Reveal.js is a web-based framework for creating interactive presentations using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Here’s a step-by-step guide to get up and running fast.

docs.title: 1. Set Up the Environment
docs.text:
You can start either by downloading Reveal.js or using a CDN. The easiest way is to use the official template from GitHub:

git clone https://github.com/hakimel/reveal.js.git
cd reveal.js
npm install
npm start

This will install dependencies and start a local server. Open http://localhost:8000 in your browser to see the default presentation.

docs.title: 2. Structure Your Slides
docs.text:
Slides in Reveal.js are just HTML <section> elements inside a <div class="slides"> container. For example:

<div class="reveal">
  <div class="slides">
    <section>Welcome to Reveal.js!</section>
    <section>
      <h2>Second Slide</h2>
      <p>Quickly create slides with HTML.</p>
    </section>
  </div>
</div>

  • Horizontal slides: New <section> inside <div class="slides">.

  • Vertical slides: Nested <section> elements inside a parent <section>.

docs.title: 3. Add Themes and Styles
docs.text:
Reveal.js comes with built-in themes. Include a theme in your HTML:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="dist/reveal.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="dist/theme/black.css">

You can also write custom CSS to match your preferred style.

docs.title: 4. Initialize Reveal.js
docs.text:
At the bottom of your HTML file, initialize the library:

<script src="dist/reveal.js"></script>
<script>
  Reveal.initialize({
    controls: true,       // show navigation arrows
    progress: true,       // show progress bar
    slideNumber: true,    // display slide numbers
    width: "100%",
    height: "100%"
  });
</script>

docs.title: 5. Add Features
docs.text:
• Markdown slides: Use data-markdown attribute to write slides in Markdown.

  • Code highlighting: Include highlight.js plugin to display formatted code.

  • Speaker notes: Add notes with <aside class="notes">Your notes here</aside>.

docs.title: 6. Share Your Presentation
docs.text:
Since Reveal.js runs in the browser, you can simply host it:

  • On GitHub Pages

  • Via any web server

  • Or as a local HTML file

All slides, styles, and assets are contained in your HTML project, making it portable and shareable.

docs.title: 7. Quick Tips
docs.text:
• Navigate slides with arrow keys, spacebar, or touch gestures.

  • Vertical slides help organize nested topics.

  • Plugins and extensions can add interactivity like charts, math equations, and embedded videos.

docs.title: 🧾 Practical Guide: Writing Good Commit Messages for Doc Sites
💡 1. General Principles
docs.text:
Good commit messages should:

  1. Explain what changed and why

  2. Use the imperative mood (“Add”, “Fix”, “Update”)

  3. Optionally include a scope in parentheses:

    • docs(site), feat(navbar), fix(link)

  4. Be short but meaningful (50 chars for title, optional longer body)

  5. Group related commits logically — avoid “misc changes”

Example format:

<type>(<scope>): <short summary>

<body explaining the change and reason, optional>

docs.title: 🧩 2. Common Commit Types (for doc sites)
docs.text: Type Meaning Example docs Documentation or content changes docs(readme): add setup guide for macOS feat Add a new feature to the site or tooling feat(search): enable full-text search with Lunr.js fix Correct a bug or broken link fix(nav): correct sidebar link for "Getting Started" style Formatting, spacing, or style change (no content change) style(css): adjust font size for code blocks refactor Reorganize structure without changing content refactor(docs): move Python tutorials into /python/ folder chore Maintenance tasks chore: update mkdocs-material to v9.5.0 ci CI/CD configuration ci: fix GitHub Pages deploy workflow build Build system or tooling build: add script to auto-generate sitemap

docs.title: 📄 A. Updating Content
docs.text:
You’re adding or revising documentation pages.

docs(python-env): add section on virtual environments
docs(opencv): rewrite introduction and add examples
docs(ai101): clarify explanation of neural networks
docs(ics): update course list and fix broken references

👉 Tip: Always mention which topic or file you changed.

docs.title: 🎨 B. Improving Site Layout or Styling
docs.text:
style(theme): adjust heading colors for better contrast
style(navbar): fix alignment on mobile
refactor(layout): move footer component to base.html
feat(ui): add dark mode toggle button

👉 Tip: These commits affect appearance or HTML/CSS structure.

docs.title: ⚙️ C. Tooling and Build System
docs.text:
chore(deps): bump mkdocs-material to 9.4.14
build(script): add auto-deploy to GitHub Pages
ci: add build check for broken links
chore: remove unused plugin `mkdocs-minify-plugin`

👉 Tip: Use these for configuration, CI/CD, or dependencies.

docs.title: 🧭 D. Fixing Errors or Links
docs.text:
fix(link): correct typo in Python tutorial URL
fix(image): update broken image path in OpenCV doc
fix(yaml): correct site_nav indentation in mkdocs.yml

👉 Tip: Use fix() when the change repairs something broken.

docs.title: 📚 E. Structural or Organizational Changes
docs.text:
refactor(structure): reorganize docs by topic
refactor(nav): simplify sidebar structure
refactor(project): merge AI101 and CS101 doc folders

👉 Tip: Use refactor() when reorganizing without changing meaning.

docs.title: 🧰 F. Meta and Configuration Files
docs.text:
docs(readme): add instructions for local preview
chore(.gitignore): ignore .DS_Store and build output
chore(config): update site_name and copyright

👉 Tip: Keep commit messages about config clean and focused.

docs.title: 🧪 G. Experiments and Temporary Updates
docs.text:
feat(experiment): test new plugin for syntax highlighting
docs(test): add placeholder section for new feature

👉 Tip: For experiments, make it clear that it’s temporary or testing.

docs.title: 📘 4. Example Commit History (Good Practice)
docs.text:
feat(navbar): add dropdown menu for course selection
docs(ics): add CPU and memory hierarchy overview
fix(link): correct reference in digital logic section
style(theme): unify heading levels and spacing
refactor(structure): split AI101 docs into subfolders
chore(deps): update mkdocs-material to 9.4.15
ci: enable auto-deploy on push to main

👉 This kind of history is:

  • Readable

  • Chronological

  • Meaningful

  • Easy to filter (you can run git log --grep=docs to see doc-related commits)

docs.title: 🧾 5. Writing Multi-line Commit Messages
docs.text:
When a change is significant, use a longer message:

docs(python-env): expand environment setup guide

Added sections on:
- Installing Python via Homebrew
- Managing multiple versions with pyenv
- Creating and activating virtual environments

Also corrected typos and improved formatting.

👉 Why: The body explains the context, so future you (or collaborators) can understand the reasoning behind the change.

docs.title: 🔐 6. Bonus Tips for Maintaining Clean History
docs.text:
• Use git add -p to stage changes selectively

  • Use git commit --amend to fix the last commit instead of making a new one

  • Use git rebase -i to squash small commits before merging

  • Write commits as if explaining to your future self

docs.title: 🧭 7. Template (You Can Copy This)
docs.text:
<type>(<scope>): <short summary>

[optional body]
- Explain what changed
- Explain why it changed
- Add context if helpful

Example:

docs(opencv): add section on cv2.imread() and cv2.imshow()

Expanded OpenCV introduction with two new examples showing
how to read and display images in Python. This improves the
clarity for beginners using Homebrew-installed Python.

docs.title: 🪄 8. Suggested Commit Scopes for Your Doc Sites
docs.text:
Project Example Scopes AI101 intro, ai-basics, vision, nlp, project-setup CS101-ICS cpu, io, memory, assembly, linux Doc-Sol office, iworks, markdown, latex, comparison General theme, site, config, nav, readme

Use consistent scopes to help future searches and automated changelogs.

docs.title: ✅ Final Tip
docs.text: Think of each commit as a micro blog post that documents your project’s evolution. A year later, good commit messages will read like a clear timeline of your learning and progress.

docs.title: 🧭 Introduction to GitHub and Best Practices
docs.text: GitHub is one of the most powerful tools for modern software development — it hosts your code, manages collaboration, tracks issues, and automates workflows. Understanding how to use GitHub effectively is essential for maintaining high-quality projects and smooth teamwork.

docs.title: 🚀 1. What is GitHub?
docs.text:
GitHub is a cloud-based platform for hosting Git repositories. It builds on Git, a distributed version control system, adding features such as:

  • Remote repositories for sharing and syncing code

  • Pull requests for proposing and reviewing changes

  • Issues and Discussions for project management

  • Actions for automation and CI/CD

  • Project boards for organizing work visually

💡 In short: Git manages your code. GitHub manages your collaboration.

docs.title: 🧩 2. Basic Git Workflow with GitHub
docs.text: A typical workflow for Git and GitHub looks like this:

docs.title: Step 1: Clone a repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/username/repository.git
cd repository

docs.title: Step 2: Create a new branch
docs.text: git checkout -b feature/my-new-feature

docs.title: Step 3: Make changes and stage them
docs.text: git add .

docs.title: Step 4: Commit your changes
docs.text: git commit -m "Add login form validation"

docs.title: Step 5: Push to GitHub
docs.text: git push origin feature/my-new-feature

docs.title: Step 6: Open a Pull Request (PR)
docs.text:
On GitHub:

  • Go to the repository

  • Click “Compare & pull request”

  • Describe your changes

  • Request a review

docs.title: Step 7: Merge and delete branch
docs.text: Once approved, merge your branch into the main branch and delete it.

docs.title: 🧠 3. Understanding GitHub Workflows
docs.text: GitHub workflows describe how teams collaborate on code. Here are some common strategies:

docs.title: 🔸 GitHub Flow (Simple and Popular)
docs.text:
Best for continuous deployment projects.

  1. Create a branch

  2. Commit changes

  3. Open a pull request

  4. Review and merge into main

  5. Deploy automatically

docs.title: 🔹 Git Flow (Structured)
docs.text:
Ideal for larger projects or release cycles.

  • main — production-ready code

  • develop — integration branch for features

  • feature/* — new features

  • release/* — preparing a release

  • hotfix/* — urgent production fixes

Git Flow adds structure but can feel heavy for smaller teams.

docs.title: 🔸 Trunk-Based Development
docs.text: All developers work on short-lived branches and merge quickly into main. Used by high-performance teams (e.g., Google, Facebook).

docs.title: ✍️ 4. Writing a Good Commit Message
docs.text: A commit message should clearly describe what and why you changed something.

docs.title: ✅ Good Practices
docs.text:
• Use the imperative mood (“Fix bug” not “Fixed bug”)

  • Limit the subject line to 50 characters

  • Use a blank line between subject and body

  • Wrap body text at 72 characters

  • Reference related issues if applicable (#42)

docs.title: ⚙️ 6. GitHub Actions (Automation Workflows)

docs.title: Introduction to SCSS (Sassy CSS)
docs.text:
SCSS — short for Sassy CSS — is a CSS preprocessor syntax that extends the capabilities of regular CSS. It allows developers to write cleaner, more maintainable, and more powerful stylesheets by introducing programming-like features such as variables, nesting, mixins, functions, and imports.

SCSS is part of the Sass (Syntactically Awesome Style Sheets) family — a project created by Hampton Catlin and developed by Natalie Weizenbaum. Today, it’s a standard tool in modern front-end development workflows, widely supported across frameworks like React, Vue, and Jekyll.

docs.title: 1. What Is SCSS?
docs.text:
SCSS is a superset of CSS3, meaning every valid CSS file is also a valid SCSS file. It compiles down to standard CSS through a Sass compiler, allowing browsers to read it normally.

// Example SCSS
$primary-color: #3498db;

body {
  background: $primary-color;
  color: white;

  h1 {
    font-size: 2rem;
  }
}
````

When compiled, it becomes:

```css
body {
  background: #3498db;
  color: white;
}
body h1 {
  font-size: 2rem;
}

docs.title: 2. SCSS vs Sass vs CSS
docs.text:
Feature CSS Sass (.sass) SCSS (.scss) Syntax Braces {} and semicolons ; Indentation-based (no braces) CSS-like (braces + semicolons) Learning Curve Easy Moderate Easy Compatibility Native to browsers Requires compiler Requires compiler Example color: red; color: red color: red;

💡 In practice, SCSS is preferred because it feels familiar to CSS developers while offering advanced features.

docs.title: 3. Why Use SCSS?
docs.text: SCSS helps you manage large, complex stylesheets efficiently. It improves readability, reusability, and consistency.

docs.title: Key Benefits
docs.text:
• Variables for consistent color and font usage

  • Nesting to mirror the structure of HTML

  • Mixins to reuse blocks of styles

  • Functions for calculations and logic

  • Imports & Partials for modular organization

  • Inheritance for shared properties among selectors

docs.title: 4. SCSS Variables
docs.text:
Variables in SCSS start with a $ symbol and store reusable values.

$font-stack: Helvetica, sans-serif;
$primary-color: #2ecc71;

body {
  font-family: $font-stack;
  color: $primary-color;
}

You can easily change the entire site’s color scheme by editing just one variable.

docs.title: 5. Nesting
docs.text:
SCSS allows nested selectors, reflecting the structure of HTML and avoiding repetitive code.

nav {
  ul {
    list-style: none;
  }
  li {
    display: inline-block;
  }
  a {
    text-decoration: none;
    color: black;
  }
}

Compiles to:

nav ul {
  list-style: none;
}
nav li {
  display: inline-block;
}
nav a {
  text-decoration: none;
  color: black;
}

⚠️ Avoid nesting more than 3 levels deep to prevent overly specific selectors.

docs.title: 6. Mixins
docs.text:
Mixins allow you to define reusable chunks of CSS code. You can also pass arguments, similar to functions.

@mixin button($color) {
  background-color: $color;
  border: none;
  border-radius: 4px;
  color: white;
  padding: 10px 15px;
}

button {
  @include button(#e74c3c);
}

This helps you maintain a consistent design system.

docs.title: 7. Functions and Operators
docs.text:
SCSS provides functions for dynamic calculations.

$base: 16px;

p {
  font-size: $base * 1.25;
}

You can also use built-in functions, like lighten(), darken(), mix(), etc.:

$color: #3498db;

button {
  background: lighten($color, 10%);
  border: 1px solid darken($color, 10%);
}

docs.title: 8. Partials and Imports
docs.text:
You can split styles into multiple files for better organization. Partial files start with an underscore (_), and they won’t compile directly.

Example structure:

scss/
  _variables.scss
  _header.scss
  _footer.scss
  main.scss

Inside main.scss:

@use 'variables';
@use 'header';
@use 'footer';

The compiler combines them into one final CSS file.

🔁 In older SCSS syntax, @import was used, but modern Sass recommends @use for better performance and namespace management.

docs.title: 9. Inheritance (@extend)
docs.text:
The @extend directive allows one selector to inherit styles from another.

.message {
  border: 1px solid #ccc;
  padding: 10px;
}

.success {
  @extend .message;
  background: #2ecc71;
}

.error {
  @extend .message;
  background: #e74c3c;
}

This reduces duplication and improves maintainability.

docs.title: 10. Control Directives
docs.text:
SCSS supports logic with @if, @for, @each, and @while directives.

$theme: dark;

body {
  @if $theme == dark {
    background: #222;
    color: white;
  } @else {
    background: white;
    color: black;
  }
}

Loops example:

@for $i from 1 through 3 {
  .item-#{$i} {
    width: 100px * $i;
  }
}

Compiles to:

.item-1 { width: 100px; }
.item-2 { width: 200px; }
.item-3 { width: 300px; }

docs.title: 11. Compilation
docs.text: SCSS needs to be compiled into CSS before browsers can read it. There are several ways to compile:

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
npm install -g sass
sass input.scss output.css

docs.title: Watch Mode
docs.text: sass --watch scss:css

docs.title: Integration
docs.text:
• Webpack / Vite: via sass-loader

  • Jekyll: automatic SCSS processing under _sass/

  • VS Code extensions: live compilation and preview

docs.title: 12. Example Project Structure
docs.text:
project/
├── scss/
│   ├── _variables.scss
│   ├── _mixins.scss
│   ├── _header.scss
│   └── main.scss
├── css/
│   └── main.css
├── index.html
└── package.json

You can configure a build script in package.json:

"scripts": {
  "build-css": "sass scss/main.scss css/main.css --style=compressed",
  "watch-css": "sass --watch scss:css"
}

Then run:

npm run watch-css

docs.title: 13. Integration with Jekyll
docs.text:
If you’re building a Jekyll site, SCSS works seamlessly:

  • Put .scss files in the _sass/ directory.

  • Reference them in your main stylesheet:

@import "variables";
@import "layout";
  • Add this to your site’s front matter:
---
---
@import "main";

Jekyll will automatically compile your SCSS into CSS when you build the site.

docs.title: 14. SCSS Best Practices
docs.text: ✅ Use variables for consistent colors and spacing ✅ Limit nesting to 3 levels ✅ Organize with partials and modular files ✅ Use @use instead of @import ✅ Keep mixins reusable and not too large ✅ Leverage functions for dynamic calculations

docs.title: 15. Example: Complete SCSS Snippet
docs.text:
// _variables.scss
$primary: #007bff;
$radius: 5px;

// _button.scss
@mixin button($bg) {
  background: $bg;
  color: white;
  border-radius: $radius;
  padding: 10px 15px;
  border: none;
}

// main.scss
@use 'variables';
@use 'button';

.btn {
  @include button($primary);
  &:hover {
    background: lighten($primary, 10%);
  }
}

Compiled CSS:

.btn {
  background: #007bff;
  color: white;
  border-radius: 5px;
  padding: 10px 15px;
  border: none;
}
.btn:hover {
  background: #339dff;
}

docs.title: 16. Conclusion
docs.text:
SCSS revolutionizes how developers write and maintain CSS. By bringing programming concepts into styling, it makes code more modular, powerful, and maintainable — especially for large projects.

For students in CS101-ICS or anyone learning modern front-end development, mastering SCSS provides a deeper understanding of modular design, style reusability, and build automation — essential concepts in professional web engineering.

  • Sass Guidelines

docs.title: Introduction to Site-Generation Technology
docs.text: Modern websites no longer have to rely solely on dynamic content rendered by server-side code. Instead, an increasingly popular approach is site generation — the process of automatically producing a complete set of static web pages from templates, data files, and structured content sources. This approach offers speed, security, and scalability, making it a preferred choice for documentation, blogs, and developer portals.

docs.title: 1. What Is Site Generation?
docs.text:
Site generation refers to the automated process of turning structured input (like Markdown files, JSON data, or templates) into a ready-to-serve static website. The process is typically handled by a static site generator (SSG) — a tool that combines layout templates with content and produces plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files.

Unlike traditional content management systems (CMS) that render pages dynamically upon each request, an SSG builds all pages in advance, often at deployment time. The generated site can then be served directly by any static file server, CDN, or cloud storage platform.

docs.title: 2. The Core Workflow
docs.text:
A typical site-generation workflow includes:

  1. Content Creation Authors write content in lightweight markup languages such as Markdown or reStructuredText.

  2. Template Rendering Templates define how content should be displayed. Variables, loops, and conditionals allow reuse of layouts across multiple pages.

  3. Static Asset Processing Generators often process CSS, JavaScript, and images, optimizing them for production.

  4. Site Output The final output is a folder of static files ready to be deployed to GitHub Pages, Netlify, or any web server.

docs.title: 3. Advantages of Static Site Generation
docs.text: Feature Description Speed Pages are prebuilt and delivered instantly without database queries. Security No database or server-side code means fewer attack surfaces. Scalability Can be distributed via global CDNs with minimal cost. Version Control Content is stored as plain text, easily tracked with Git. Portability Works offline and can be deployed to many platforms.

docs.title: 4. Common Site Generators
docs.text:
Several popular tools exist for different use cases: je

Generator Language Typical Use Jekyll Ruby Personal blogs and GitHub Pages Hugo Go Fast builds for large sites MkDocs Python Documentation sites (especially with Material for MkDocs) Docusaurus JavaScript Developer documentation with React integration Next.js (Static Export) JavaScript Hybrid static and dynamic content Eleventy (11ty) JavaScript Simple, flexible, template-based blogs

Each generator follows the same principle but offers different templating languages, plugin ecosystems, and build pipelines.

docs.title: 5. Static vs. Dynamic Websites
docs.text:
Aspect Static Site (Generated) Dynamic Site (Server-Rendered) Content Source Markdown or JSON Database queries Rendering Pre-build time On-demand per request Performance Very fast Depends on backend Maintenance Low Higher (requires backend upkeep) Typical Use Docs, blogs, portfolios Forums, e-commerce, dashboards

Many modern frameworks (like Next.js and Astro) now combine both worlds through hybrid rendering, where some pages are static and others are dynamic.

docs.title: 6. The Modern Web Ecosystem
docs.text:
Static site generation has evolved into a central part of the Jamstack architecture — an approach based on:

  • JavaScript for interactivity

  • APIs for dynamic data access

  • Markup for prebuilt HTML pages

Jamstack decouples the frontend from backend services, enabling developers to create fast, modular, and secure web experiences.

docs.title: 7. Deployment and Hosting
docs.text:
Static sites can be hosted almost anywhere. Common options include:

  • GitHub Pages — free hosting for personal and project sites

  • Netlify — continuous deployment from Git repositories

  • Vercel — optimized for Next.js and frontend frameworks

  • Cloudflare Pages — integrated CDN delivery

  • AWS S3 + CloudFront — enterprise-grade scalability

Deployment is often automated via CI/CD pipelines that trigger site rebuilds whenever content or code changes.

docs.title: 8. Example: Building a Documentation Site
docs.text:
Suppose you write Markdown documentation for a course like Introduction to Computer Systems. Using MkDocs:

pip install mkdocs-material
mkdocs new cs101-docs
cd cs101-docs
mkdocs serve

Then you can edit Markdown files in the docs/ directory, and MkDocs will automatically rebuild the site. When ready to publish:

mkdocs build
mkdocs gh-deploy

Your entire documentation site is generated and deployed to GitHub Pages.

docs.title: 9. Conclusion
docs.text:
Site-generation technology represents a shift toward simpler, faster, and more maintainable web development. By separating content from presentation and building pages ahead of time, developers gain the benefits of version control, reproducibility, and performance — all while avoiding the complexity of traditional dynamic servers.

Whether for technical documentation, personal blogs, or academic websites, static site generation provides a modern, efficient, and elegant foundation for publishing on the web.

Further Reading:

  • Jamstack.org

  • MkDocs Documentation

  • Hugo Static Site Generator

  • Jekyll Official Site

docs.title: Introduction to Jekyll
docs.text:
Jekyll is one of the most influential and widely used static site generators (SSGs). Originally created by Tom Preston-Werner, the co-founder of GitHub, Jekyll powers GitHub Pages, the free hosting service that allows users to publish websites directly from their Git repositories.

Jekyll is written in Ruby and designed to transform plain text—typically Markdown files—into a complete static website. Its philosophy is simple: "No database, no CMS, just files."

docs.title: 1. What Is Jekyll?
docs.text:
Jekyll converts structured text content (like Markdown or HTML) combined with templates (written in Liquid, a Ruby-based templating language) into a ready-to-deploy static site composed of plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

It follows a straightforward workflow:

  1. You write your content in Markdown.
  2. You define templates and layouts in HTML with placeholders.
  3. You run the jekyll build command to generate static pages.
  4. You deploy the _site folder to your web host or GitHub Pages.

In essence, Jekyll acts as a content compiler — turning your text files into a full website.

docs.title: 2. Key Features
docs.text: Feature Description Markdown Support Write content using simple Markdown syntax. Liquid Templating Use variables, loops, and conditionals to build flexible layouts. Front Matter Add metadata (title, date, layout) to the top of each page or post. Collections & Data Files Organize custom types of content beyond posts and pages. Permalinks & URLs Configure how URLs are generated for posts and pages. Plugins & Themes Extend functionality or customize appearance easily. GitHub Pages Integration Deploy automatically via GitHub’s built-in Jekyll support.

docs.title: 3. Directory Structure
docs.text:
A typical Jekyll project looks like this:


my-site/  
├── _config.yml # Main configuration file  
├── _posts/ # Blog posts (Markdown files)  
│ ├── 2025-11-10-hello-world.md  
├── _layouts/ # Layout templates  
│ ├── default.html  
│ ├── post.html  
├── _includes/ # Reusable HTML snippets  
├── _data/ # YAML or JSON data files  
├── _site/ # Generated static site (output folder)  
├── assets/ # Images, CSS, JS  
└── index.md # Home page content

````

Each part serves a specific purpose:
- `_layouts/` defines the overall HTML structure.  
- `_includes/` contains reusable components like headers or footers.  
- `_posts/` stores blog articles named by date convention.  
- `_site/` is generated by Jekyll and should not be manually edited.

---

## 4. Front Matter

Every Jekyll page or post starts with a **YAML front matter block**, which stores metadata.

Example:

```markdown
---
layout: post
title: "Hello Jekyll"
date: 2025-11-10
author: Matt Li
tags: [jekyll, web, cs101]
---

This is my first post using **Jekyll**!
````

The variables defined here can be accessed in templates, making Jekyll highly customizable.

---

## 5. Liquid Templating

Jekyll uses **Liquid**, a template language created by Shopify, to render dynamic content during site generation.

Example:

```html
<h1>{{ page.title }}</h1>
<p>Published on {{ page.date | date: "%B %d, %Y" }}</p>

{% for post in site.posts %}
  <li><a href="{{ post.url }}">{{ post.title }}</a></li>
{% endfor %}

Liquid provides:

  • {{ variable }} for output

  • {% tag %} for logic (loops, conditionals)

  • Filters (like date, upcase, truncate) for formatting

docs.title: 6. Configuration (_config.yml)
docs.text:
The _config.yml file defines site-wide settings.

Example:

title: My CS101 Notes
description: A personal documentation site built with Jekyll
baseurl: "" # the subpath, e.g. /blog
url: "https://mattli.github.io"

theme: minima
markdown: kramdown

plugins:
  - jekyll-feed
  - jekyll-seo-tag

You can control output directories, Markdown processors, plugins, and URL structures all from this file.

docs.title: Blog Posts
docs.text:
Save posts in _posts/ with filenames like YYYY-MM-DD-title.md.

Example:

---
layout: post
title: "Introduction to Static Site Generators"
date: 2025-11-10
---

Static site generators are tools that build websites from plain text.

Jekyll automatically lists them by date under site.posts.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Pages (like about.md or contact.md) can live in the root directory or subfolders. They also use front matter but are not listed as posts.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
Jekyll supports themes that define styles and layouts. Install a theme from RubyGems:

gem install jekyll-theme-cayman

Then, in _config.yml:

theme: jekyll-theme-cayman

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
Plugins extend Jekyll’s functionality — from generating sitemaps to adding search support.

Example:

gem install jekyll-seo-tag

and in _config.yml:

plugins:
  - jekyll-seo-tag

docs.title: 9. Building and Serving the Site
docs.text:
To create and view your Jekyll site locally:

gem install bundler jekyll
jekyll new my-site
cd my-site
bundle exec jekyll serve

Then visit:

http://localhost:4000

Jekyll will automatically rebuild your site each time you save a file.

To generate the static files manually:

bundle exec jekyll build

The output appears in the _site/ directory.

docs.title: 10. Deploying to GitHub Pages
docs.text:
One of Jekyll’s greatest strengths is native GitHub Pages integration. Simply push your site repository to GitHub, and GitHub automatically builds and serves your site.

Steps:

  1. Create a new repository named <username>.github.io

  2. Push your Jekyll site to the repository

  3. Enable GitHub Pages in repository settings (if needed)

Your website will be live at:

https://<username>.github.io

For project pages, push to the gh-pages branch or use GitHub Actions for CI/CD automation.

docs.title: ✅ Advantages
docs.text:
• Fully static, fast, and secure

  • Easy to host (especially on GitHub Pages)

  • Simple text-based workflow (Markdown + Git)

  • Flexible templating system

  • Strong plugin and theme ecosystem

docs.title: ⚠️ Limitations
docs.text:
• Requires Ruby environment (setup can be tricky for beginners)

  • No built-in dynamic features (e.g., comments need third-party services)

  • Rebuilding the entire site for every change can be slow on very large projects

docs.title: 12. Example: Building a Personal Blog
docs.text:
To build a blog quickly:

jekyll new myblog
cd myblog
bundle exec jekyll serve

Then edit _config.yml and add posts under _posts/. You can customize the layout in _layouts/ and publish it directly to GitHub Pages.

docs.title: 13. Jekyll in the Modern Web
docs.text: Although newer tools like Hugo, Next.js, and Eleventy have emerged, Jekyll remains foundational in static site development. Its simplicity, transparency, and deep GitHub integration make it an ideal choice for educational projects, personal blogs, and documentation sites—such as CS101-ICS.

docs.title: 14. Conclusion
docs.text:
Jekyll embodies the philosophy of minimalism and automation in web publishing. By separating content, layout, and configuration, it provides developers with a clean, reproducible way to build static websites that are fast, reliable, and easy to maintain.

For students and developers, learning Jekyll is an excellent introduction to static site generation, Git-based workflows, and the broader concepts behind the Jamstack architecture.

  • Jekyll on GitHub Pages

  • Liquid Template Language

  • Jekyll Themes Directory
